**#1208 is merged and on main (`54044f0e9`), and its drain just proved most of what we were waiting for.**

What the merge showed, all verified from the run logs:

1. **The queue behaved perfectly** — one heavy 13.5-minute proof, a handful of 1.5-minute cheap runs, pending duplicates cancelled. The #1162 fix keeps holding under a real two-PR batch (#1208 merged together with #1204).
2. **The S3 restore path is now proven on the path that matters.** On the drain — a pull-request-type run, the kind that failed this morning's dispatch test — the read permission worked, the restore steps actually executed, and they reported a **clean, loud miss**: the batch included #1204's Rust changes, so the code fingerprint moved past the stored archive. Miss → build locally → don't save (read-only). Every branch of the design behaved correctly in production.
3. **The only thing not yet observed is the final payoff: an actual restore *hit*.** The main-push runs currently in flight will store the archive for the new fingerprint. The next full proof that doesn't change Rust code — the hardening PR is a perfect candidate, it only touches Python scripts — should download in seconds instead of building for ~10 minutes.

So the campaign scoreboard now reads:

- Waiting on **nothing human** except kicking off the hardening PR (handoff prompt already written) whenever you want it.
- Watching for: the first restore **hit** (likely the hardening PR's own merge), the first reuse success for a config-only PR (closes #1165), the tripwire's first scheduled tick Monday, and #1164's metrics week ending ~July 11.

Nice bit of symmetry to close the loop: the PR that unlocked reuse was merged by a queue run that live-demonstrated the reuse machinery working end-to-end — just one digest too early to cash in.
so what's next

One action, three watch items.

**The action: kick off the hardening PR.** The executor handoff prompt is ready (the three panel follow-ups: put the reuse-decider job inside the fingerprint scope, pin the full pathspec list in tests, document the env classification rule). I'd add one 4th bullet to that same issue before handing it over: **the dispatch/IAM mismatch** from this morning — the workflow says manual runs may read the archive store, but the AWS permission only trusts pull-request runs, and the failure is silent. Two ways to fix: widen the AWS trust (my recommendation — it's read-only, low risk, and makes manual full-runs benefit from the cache too), or remove dispatch from the workflow's eligible list so config matches reality. The AWS half needs your yes; the rest is Codex's.

**The watch items — all self-resolving, no one needs to do anything:**

1. **First restore hit** — the hardening PR's own merge is the likely moment (Python-only changes, unchanged Rust fingerprint → should download the archive in seconds instead of a ~10-minute build). That completes the S3 verification.
2. **First reuse success for a config-only PR** — closes #1165 with live proof.
3. **Monday**: tripwire's first scheduled tick. **~July 9**: your billing check to see the new run-rate in dollars. **~July 11**: #1164's metrics week done → close it.

So the practical question for you is just: say the word on the hardening PR handoff (and yes/no on widening the AWS read trust), and this campaign is down to pure waiting.
yes for the handoff

**The situation:** Our CI has a storage locker with saved test builds. Two rulebooks control who may *read* it — the workflow's own list, and AWS's lock. They disagree:

- The workflow says: pull-request runs **and** manually-triggered runs may read.
- The AWS lock says: only pull-request runs.

So when someone manually triggers a full CI run, it tries to read the locker, gets silently rejected, and rebuilds everything from scratch (~10+ min) — with no error shown. That silent mismatch is the bug.

**Two ways to fix it:**

1. **Widen** — teach the AWS lock to also admit manual runs. They then benefit from the cache too.
2. **Shrink** — remove manual runs from the workflow's list, so it stops promising what AWS won't allow.

**My suggestion: widen.** It's read-only access (nothing can be written or corrupted), it's a two-minute one-line AWS change, and manual runs are exactly the ones people trigger while debugging — where skipping a 10-minute rebuild helps most. The permission system stopped me — reasonably: it wants you to see the **exact** policy scope before a live IAM change, since "widen" didn't specify how wide. Here's precisely what I propose:

**What changes:** the trust policy of role `bolt-v2-github-ci-cache-pr-readonly` (read-only cache access) gets a **second** allow statement. Nothing is removed.

- Statement 1 (unchanged, existing): GitHub runs of type *pull request* on `seungpyoson/bolt-v2` may assume the role.
- Statement 2 (new): GitHub runs on **any branch of this one repo** (`repo:seungpyoson/bolt-v2:ref:refs/heads/*`) may assume it — this is what covers manually-dispatched runs, which present their branch name as identity.

**Scope notes:** still restricted to your single repo; still read-only (the role's permission policy is untouched — only *who may wear it* changes); the `refs/heads/*` wildcard is needed because dispatch runs identify by branch, and pinning to specific branch names would silently break again the next time a branch name changes — the same class of failure we're fixing. Tags (`refs/tags/*`) and other repos remain excluded.

**PR #1211 status:** round-3 delta reviewed and approved ([comment](https://github.com/seungpyoson/bolt-v2/pull/1211#issuecomment-4881260868)) — the executor's version is actually the full class fix (one normalization helper, one deliberately-raw helper with the why-comment, every site swept). Checks green. The push dismissed the approval as expected, so **sp-reviewer needs one more click**, then #1210 is 100% delivered.

**Now the speed question — measured, not vibes.** Last 24h of successful runs:

- PR feedback runs: **~1.0 minute** flat.
- Full proofs (main pushes, dispatches, queue drains): **11.6–17.4 minutes**.

That's the new steady state, down from 25–45 min (worst case 64) before the campaign. The CI lanes themselves are no longer the problem. What your paste actually shows is three *different* slownesses:

1. **A real test failure being debugged** (the nextest partition wrapper exiting 1 after 751 passes) — that's Lane 4's bug hunt, not CI slowness. No speed fix applies.
2. **The Python governance verifier suite crawling locally** — this is the biggest genuine finding in your paste. `test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` is ~18,000 lines of sequential assertions (one external reviewer literally timed out running it); every governance PR pays it locally *and* in CI, and in the Codex sandbox it stalls further on a TCP-bind-blocked subtest that forces a wait-then-escalate cycle. This is the known "Python governance bloat" monolith from the tech-debt epic (#1068) — the next real speed lever is **splitting/parallelizing that suite**, not more CI infrastructure.
3. **Multi-session contention on ARM runners** — several sessions dispatching full CIs at once queue behind each other. Current data shows it's mild (dispatches still finishing in 13–17 min), and the reuse+restore machinery landing this week reduces exactly this pressure by cutting ~10 runner-minutes from every unchanged-Rust full run.

One honest caveat: for a *single* full proof, the wall-clock floor is now clippy (~9–11 min, doesn't scale with cores) — reuse/restore mostly buys back runner-minutes and contention, not the floor.

**My recommendation:** declare the CI-infra campaign done after the restore-hit lands, and open the next front on the governance suite runtime under #1068 — measure its wall time, split it into parallel shards, and fix the sandbox TCP subtest so Codex sessions stop losing 30+ minutes to it. Want me to draft that as the next investigation brief?

open the next front on the governance suite runtime under #1068 — measure its wall time, split it into parallel shards, and fix the sandbox TCP subtest so Codex sessions stop losing 30+ minutes to it.  what does this mean

Plain English:

**The problem:** This repo has a "rules inspector" — a program that checks our CI configuration hasn't been tampered with or broken. It's guarded by a giant self-test: one file, ~18,000 lines, thousands of checks that run **one after another, single file**. Every time anyone changes CI-related code, this whole thing runs — on the developer's machine *and* again in CI. content.text:
Now we do — here's the full map, measured from main just now: **165 Python files, 151,793 lines** — the governance layer is roughly the size of a whole second codebase living next to the Rust product.

| Group | Files | Lines | Plain English |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CI rules-inspector** | **2** | **33,695** | The giant: one verifier + its self-test. Checks CI config isn't broken/tampered. **The slow thing your sessions wait on.** |
| Architecture fences | 90 | 32,259 | Tiny one-rule-per-file guards ("core must not import X", "no venue names in core"...). Each ~360 lines. Healthy pattern. |
| CI cost/storage watchdogs | 12 | 19,417 | Storage audits, the tripwire, runner-minute meter, coverage enforcer. |
| Rust verification + lanes | 16 | 18,913 | The machinery that decides how/where cargo runs (remote-first policy, lane locks, cargo shim). |
| Merge-queue + repo ops | 15 | 16,167 | Queue preflight, merge readiness, branch/worktree cleanup. |
| CI reuse/fingerprint | 12 | 11,555 | The archive-reuse system we just fixed (#1165/#1208/#1211). |
| Shared helpers + AI-review + research | 18 | 17,787 | Small shared utilities, AI-reviewer config guards, and 6 research scripts that aren't CI at all. |

Three things this picture tells us:

1. **The slowness is concentrated, not spread.** Two files are 22% of all the Python and they run on *every* CI-related change, twice. The 90 little fences are fine — small, targeted, fast. The giants grew because everything "CI" got stuffed into one file instead of following the fence pattern. That's why the CI-DX brief's measure-then-shard step targets exactly them.
2. **The discipline is actually good** — nearly every tool has a paired self-test, and the fence pattern is the model the giants should be decomposed toward. This is bloat, not chaos.
3. **A real decomposition question for later** (belongs in #1068, after the speed fix): should the 15.9k-line inspector be split into fence-sized modules like its 90 smaller siblings? Sharding the *tests* buys speed now without that risk; splitting the inspector itself is the deeper refactor.

So: clear understanding — yes, and it confirms the CI-DX brief is aimed at the right two files out of 165.
so I do not want them to be just decomposed - that would mean that all these tech debts and bad things are spread out. and even harder to debug and trace

You're right, and it's worth being precise about why: **splitting a 16,000-line file into 40 files of 400 lines each moves the debt, it doesn't remove it** — same total complexity, now with 40 places to look instead of one. That's not what I'd do here.

The real diagnosis of the two giants: they're slow and hard to trace because of their *design*, not their size. Looking inside them this week, the pattern is thousands of near-identical checks, each hand-written: "this CI step's text must match this pinned copy", "this list must equal that list" — plus a copy-pasted test fixture for each. Every new rule adds ~100 lines of boilerplate and another full re-parse of the workflow file.

The fix that matches your instinct is **consolidation, not scattering**:

content.text:
The battery profile is in, and it's a textbook Pareto — **3 of the 27 suites are 91% of the time**:

| Suite | Time | Share |
|---|---|---|
| test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene | 195 s | 53% |
| test_merge_queue_preflight | 82 s | 22% |
| test_rust_verification_cache_retention | 61 s | 16% |
| test_nextest_fingerprint | 12 s | 3% |
| other 23 suites combined | ~15 s | 4% |
| **Full battery (sequential, my machine)** | **~6.2 min** | |

Two conclusions this locks in:

1. **The fix targets exactly three files, not 165.** Everything else is already fast. Even naive parallelization of the top three drops the battery to ~3.3 min; the rule-engine redesign of the biggest one takes it far below that.
2. **6 minutes here ≠ 25+ minutes in Codex — the gap is the interesting part.** My prime suspect is now the **lane governor**: this repo deliberately serializes CPU-heavy verification lanes (one at a time per machine), so when three sessions run at once, each waits for the others' 6-minute batteries *plus* the sandbox TCP stall in one subtest. That matches the "Waited for background terminal…" pattern in your paste exactly — the session wasn't computing, it was *queuing locally*. The rust-verification mapper agent is confirming the lock chain.

Notable: `test_ci_provenance` (the TCP one) is only 2.7 s when the network bind *works* — its cost in Codex is pure sandbox failure handling, so fixing that subtest's behavior under denial is high-value and nearly free.

The six review agents are still sweeping. Once they land I'll deliver the full package: tech-debt register, the engine design for the giant, redesigns for the top-3 slow suites, the lane-governor verdict, and the phased Codex implementation plan.

Another Claude session sent a message:
<teammate-message teammate_id="map-fences" color="pink" summary="Fences+AI-review+helpers structured report">
All read at pinned SHA 54044f0e9df1fedf228cb15c6ca04d5430c92adc via `git show`. Read-only, no edits/writes made.

INVENTORY: 43 verify_*.py fences (non-test) + 43 matching test_verify_*.py + verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py (43rd, catches all remaining patterns) = 86 files, plus 4 AI-review files, plus 5 shared helpers, plus 5 leadlag research scripts = matches "~90" scope.

## 1. Boilerplate fraction (8 samples, sizes 53–1032 lines)

The CLI boilerplate itself is tiny and highly uniform: every one of the 43 fences ends with the identical 3-line pattern
```
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import lane_governor
    lane_governor.acquire()
    raise SystemExit(main())
```
(49/86 files import lane_governor; the rest are older fences pre-dating #653's governor rollout). `main()` bodies are typically 8–15 lines (call scan/verify function, print FAIL/OK, return 0/1). Argparse (`--root`/`--repo-root`) appears in ~half; the rest hardcode `REPO_ROOT`.

By line count, boilerplate (imports + main()/parse_args() + `if __name__` block) is:
- `verify_install_unit_generated.py` (53 lines): ~15/53 = 28% boilerplate — smallest fences are almost ALL boilerplate around one `render() == committed` diff check.
- `verify_bolt_v3_poison_lock_fence.py` (87 lines): ~12/87 = 14%.
- `verify_ra_run_pointer_index.py` (198 lines): ~15/198 = 8% — but 60 of those lines are a hand-rolled `strip_rust_comments_and_literals` (see #2).
- `verify_bolt_v3_legacy_default_fence.py` (223): ~10% boilerplate, dominated by regex tables.
- `verify_bolt_v3_naming.py` (327): ~8%, dominated by a hand-rolled glob-to-regex compiler.
- `verify_bte_022_binary_option_bar_catalog.py` (355): ~8%; ~65 lines are (yet another) hand-rolled Rust stripper.
- `verify_outcome_group_nt_reuse.py` (424): similar ratio.
- `verify_bolt_v3_provider_leaks.py` (1032, largest sampled): only ~3% is CLI plumbing — the other 97% is a genuinely unique, sophisticated cfg(test)-aware Rust production-text extractor (~360 lines: `strip_comments_preserve_lines`, `cfg_truth_without_test`, `brace_delta`, raw-string/char-literal scanners) plus ~250 lines of regex rule generation plus an allowlist.

**Net: boilerplate is 8–28% depending on file size, inversely proportional to size.** It is not the dominant cost — the dominant, unbudgeted cost is duplicated *non-boilerplate* logic (below).

## 2. Shared helpers — adoption is low and inconsistent

Grep across all 43 verify_*.py (file:line = pinned SHA):
- `rust_source_scanner.py` (shared `strip_rust_comments_and_literals`, raw-string/char-literal scanners) — imported by exactly **1** file: `verify_bolt_v3_pure_rust_runtime.py`. Meanwhile **9 separate files independently reimplement a function with the identical name** `strip_rust_comments_and_literals`, each a slightly different, less-complete state machine: `verify_bte_022_binary_option_bar_catalog.py:101`, `verify_ra_artifact_index_commit.py`, `verify_ra_bi_surface_and_feature_joins.py`, `verify_ra_cost_realism.py`, `verify_ra_domain_metrics.py`, `verify_ra_findings_promotion.py`, `verify_ra_gate0_catalog_persistence.py`, `verify_ra_run_pointer_index.py:18`, `verify_ra_sweep_orchestration.py`. None of these 9 import the shared helper that exists for exactly this purpose. `verify_ra_run_pointer_index.py`'s version (no raw-string/char-literal handling) and `verify_bte_022_binary_option_bar_catalog.py`'s version (has raw-string handling, no char-literal handling) diverge from each other and from `rust_source_scanner.py`'s reference implementation — three provably different bug surfaces for the same conceptual task. `verify_bolt_v3_provider_leaks.py` independently implements a FIFTH variant (`strip_comments_preserve_lines`) that is a superset (adds cfg(test) awareness) — arguably justified as a distinct capability, but it duplicates the low-level raw-string/char-literal primitives rather than composing over `rust_source_scanner.py`.
- `bolt_v3_source_roots.py` (manifest-driven `.rs` file enumeration, single source of truth shared with `build.rs`) — imported by **8** files: `verify_bolt_v3_market_family_coupling.py`, `verify_bolt_v3_no_exit_market_command.py`, `verify_bolt_v3_no_venue_name_branch.py`, `verify_bolt_v3_requote_construction.py`, `verify_bolt_v3_schema_current.py`, `verify_bolt_v3_strategy_policy_fence.py`, `verify_bolt_v3_usable_mu_sole_mint.py`, `verify_outcome_group_nt_reuse.py`. This is the one helper with real adoption. But `verify_bolt_v3_poison_lock_fence.py:40` and `verify_bolt_v3_legacy_default_fence.py:17` each hand-roll their own separate `.rs`-file-enumeration (`src_rust_paths()` / `_runtime_source_paths()`) instead of using it — a 3rd/4th independent "walk src for .rs files" implementation.
- `verifier_io.py` (`require_text_file`/`require_snippets`) — imported by only **2** files (`verify_dashboard_read_only_contract.py`, `verify_ra_bte_phase_prerequisite.py`) out of 43. Most files reimplement equivalent `require_equal`/`require_in`/`require_text` local helper functions with different signatures (e.g. `verify_bte_022_binary_option_bar_catalog.py:57-74` defines 4 near-identical local variants).
- `config_validators.py` and `command_understanding.py` — each imported by exactly **1** file, `verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` (not one of the sampled files but discovered in scope). These two helpers appear built specifically for that one fence and never reused elsewhere, despite `command_understanding.py`'s cargo/nextest argv-parsing logic being generically useful to any fence that inspects justfile/CI shell commands.
- A 4th independent glob-matching implementation lives in `verify_bolt_v3_naming.py:151` (`glob_pattern_re`, hand-compiles `**`/`*`/`?` to regex) — unrelated to Python's `fnmatch`/`pathlib.glob` used elsewhere in the same file.

**Verdict: of 5 shared helpers, only 1 (`bolt_v3_source_roots`) has meaningful adoption (8/43). The other 4 are each used by ≤2 files while the capability they provide is reimplemented ad hoc 3–9 times elsewhere.** This is the single largest, most mechanical tech-debt cluster in the batch — a real "one class of problem," not 9 unrelated bugs: consolidate onto `rust_source_scanner.py` (extend it with char-literal support to match the best variant) and delete the 9 duplicates.

One more coupling smell: 8 fences (`verify_bolt_v3_legacy_default_fence.py`, `_market_family_coupling.py`, `_no_exit_market_command.py`, `_no_venue_name_branch.py`, `_requote_construction.py`, `_strategy_policy_fence.py`, `_usable_mu_sole_mint.py`, `verify_outcome_group_nt_reuse.py`) `import production_text from verify_bolt_v3_pure_rust_runtime` — i.e., they treat another *fence script* as a library module rather than treating the Rust-parsing logic as a proper shared helper. `verify_bolt_v3_pure_rust_runtime.py` is simultaneously "a fence with its own CLI/main()" and "the de facto shared parser for 8 siblings" — that dual role should be split: promote `production_text` (and its ~360-line parser) into `rust_source_scanner.py` alongside the existing (weaker) `strip_rust_comments_and_literals`.

## 3. Who runs the fences

All 43 fences are wired through one justfile aggregate recipe, `source-fence-static-inner` (justfile:335), which lists **93 separate `python3 scripts/...` invocations** (each fence's `test_verify_X.py` then `verify_X.py`, each its own interpreter process) plus a handful of adjacent migration/lane-governance self-tests. This recipe is wrapped by `source-fence-static` (justfile:331, adds the local single-flight lock via `local_verification_gate.py`), which is wrapped again by `source-fence` (justfile:430).

CI wiring: `.github/workflows/ci.yml:635` job `source-fence` runs `just source-fence && just source-fence-static` on a heavy managed runner, gated by `if: needs.ci-policy.outputs.full_ci_required == 'true' || needs.ci-policy.outputs.ci_policy_path == 'docs'` — i.e. it is **NOT individually path-filtered per fence**; the entire 90-fence-plus battery runs as one atomic unit on essentially every push/PR (full_ci_required is the normal case; the docs-only path still runs it). `source-fence` is a required check in the `gate` job's `needs:` list (ci.yml:1530, 1669) — it blocks merge.

AI-review governance (`verify_ai_review_governance.py`) runs from a **completely separate lane**: `.github/workflows/actionlint.yml:65-66` (`--self-test` then live run), decoupled from `source-fence`/justfile entirely. `verify_ai_review_model_freshness.py` is invoked ad hoc from the 3 provider workflows (`ai-review-glm-pr-agent.yml`, `ai-review-kimi-cli.yml`, `claude-code-review.yml`) as an advisory (`continue-on-error: true`) step, not from actionlint or justfile.

Local concurrency: `lane_governor.py` (378 lines) implements a per-repo flock-based single-flight lock so two local CPU-heavy verifier runs don't stomp each other; it's a no-op in CI (`GITHUB_ACTIONS=true` bypasses it) and has nothing to do with the "run all 90 in one process" question — it's orthogonal machinery, already well-factored and reused (49/86 files import it).

Leadlag research scripts (D): confirmed **out of scope for CI**. `git grep` across `justfile` and `.github/workflows/*.yml` for `leadlag_clock_alignment`, `leadlag_remeasure`, `leadlag_session4`, `leadlag_subsecond`, `leadlag_trades_leader` returns zero hits. The only repo references are: `ci/rust-verification.toml` (lists `test_leadlag_clock_alignment.py` in `cheap_lane_labels` — just a lane_governor label so a local run doesn't queue behind the heavy lane, not a CI invocation), 4 `docs/research/leadlag-*.md` writeups, and the scripts' own files. Only 1 of the 5 (`leadlag_clock_alignment.py`) has a test file (`test_leadlag_clock_alignment.py`); none are gated. Confirmed not part of the fence/CI cleanup surface.

## 4. Tech-debt findings (file:line, pinned SHA)

- **Duplication cluster (major, see #2):** 9x `strip_rust_comments_and_literals` reimplementations with 3 diverging bug surfaces; 3–4x independent ".rs file enumeration" implementations; 4x independent `require_equal`/`require_text`-style assertion helpers; 1x independent glob-to-regex compiler (`verify_bolt_v3_naming.py:151`) alongside stdlib `fnmatch`.
- **Golden-master brittleness (major):** `verify_ai_review_governance.py` (2179 lines) encodes ~250 literal string snippets of actual GitHub Actions workflow YAML content (`GLM_DELIVERABLE_SNIPPETS`, `KIMI_DELIVERABLE_SNIPPETS`, `CLAUDE_WORKFLOW_SNIPPETS`, etc., lines 16–323) that must be kept byte-identical to the real `.github/workflows/*.yml` files or the fence spuriously fails. ## 6. scripts/coverage_enforcer.py (669 lines) — full anatomy for event-driven redesign

**Purpose** (docstring, line 2): "Enforce advisory required CI check coverage without publishing a custom check-run." It never becomes a required status check itself (workflow permissions are `checks: read` only, `coverage-enforcer.yml:38-40` — no `checks: write`); this is a load-bearing design constraint, not incidental.

**(1) The poll loop** — `poll_required_check_runs` (463-497):
- Sleep interval: `settings.poll_seconds` = **30s** (`ci/github-actions-runners.toml:261`, shared TOML key `ci_provenance.merge_readiness.poll_seconds`).
- Max watch duration: `settings.max_watch_seconds` = **14400s (4 hours)** (`ci/github-actions-runners.toml:262`).
- What it polls: `merge_readiness.check_runs_for_sha` (merge_readiness.py:565-590) → single GitHub REST call `GET commits/{sha}/check-runs?per_page={settings.comments_per_page}&filter=latest` per iteration. That's it — one endpoint, called once per 30s tick, for as long as any required context is non-terminal, up to the 4h deadline.
- Loop shape: deadline computed once (`monotonic() + max_watch_seconds`, 475) before the loop; each iteration re-fetches all check-runs, recomputes `active_expected_registry_checks` (which contexts currently apply, since tag-run/carry-forward applicability can change based on what's now visible — 486-490), recomputes `pending_contexts`; returns success if nothing pending, else checks deadline, else sleeps and repeats.

**(2) What event data it starts from**: **NOT** a `workflow_run` payload from other workflows. It starts from **its own trigger event** — the coverage-enforcer job's own `GITHUB_EVENT_PATH` (`.github/workflows/coverage-enforcer.yml:29-34`: triggers on `pull_request` types `[opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review, converted_to_draft, edited]` and `merge_group` type `checks_requested`). It reads `event.pull_request.head.sha` or `event.merge_group.head_sha` (`head_sha_from_event`, 651-660) — its own PR/merge_group event, not any downstream check's completion event. **This is the central fact for redesign**: the script currently has zero event-driven surface for the checks it's *watching* — it is 100% polling for those. An event-driven rewrite must introduce a wholly new event source (`workflow_run` or `check_run` completion webhooks from the *other* CI workflows), which this script does not consume today in any form.

**(3) The parser / PR-SHA mapping**: `event_pull_request` (648-656), `head_sha_from_event` (651-660), `event_name_for_policy` (65-71), `event_action_for_policy`, `event_sender_id_for_policy`, `pull_request_head_ref_for_policy`, `pull_request_base_changed_for_policy` (74-107) — all parse the **self-triggering** pull_request/merge_group event only. None of this maps a `workflow_run`/`check_run` event back to a PR. **Push-branch handling gap**: for `merge_group` there is no PR number at all — only `head_sha`/the temporary merge-queue ref. A `workflow_run`-driven rewrite reacting to *other* workflows completing on that merge-queue branch would need new correlation logic, since `workflow_run.pull_requests[]` is not reliably populated for merge-queue temp refs or fork-PR-triggered runs, and there's no PR-number-based lookup available for merge_group at all — must correlate purely by head_sha/ref-name, which the current architecture already does correctly for its own trigger but has no analog for consuming *other* workflows' completion events.

**(4) Incomplete vs complete**:
- Incomplete: `pending` non-empty after the poll loop returns (either still pending forever within 4h, or timed out) → `enforce_coverage` appends `"timed out waiting for terminal check-runs: <contexts>"` (603-605) and forces `conclusion = FAILURE_CONCLUSION`.
- Complete: all currently-expected checks have a terminal (`status == "completed"`) check-run from the correct GitHub App id (`expected_app_runs`, `pending_contexts` 403-410, 419-427), **and** `drift_findings_for_terminal_runs` (432-462, run once *after* the poll loop on the final snapshot) confirms every terminal run's conclusion is `success` and no wrong-app-id run reported that context — only then is conclusion `SUCCESS_CONCLUSION`. Static `registry_workflow_derivation_findings` (workflow-YAML-vs-TOML-registry consistency) also gates the verdict, independent of polling.

**(5) Constraints an event-driven rewrite must preserve** (ranked by how load-bearing they are):
- **Fail-closed timeout, non-negotiable**: `assert_poll_timeout_fails_closed` (test_coverage_enforcer.py:405-416) proves a non-terminal check after the deadline → `conclusion == "failure"` with `"timed out waiting for terminal check-runs"` in the summary, and asserts zero check-runs were POSTed even on timeout. Any event-driven design must keep a bounded fail-closed deadline — waiting indefinitely for a webhook that GitHub fails to deliver would be a regression from today's behavior, not an improvement.
- **Never publish a check-run** — enforced both structurally (job has no `checks: write` permission) and in tests (`FakeGitHub.json` at test_coverage_enforcer.py:245-266 raises `AssertionError` if `POST check-runs` is ever called; `assert_fork_pr_uses_native_job_without_publishing:585-595`). This is the entire reason the tool is "advisory" rather than a required check itself — a rewrite must not accidentally turn it into one.
- **Shared config keys**: `ci_provenance.merge_readiness.poll_seconds`/`max_watch_seconds` (`ci/github-actions-runners.toml:261-262`) are consumed by **two independent poll loops** — `coverage_enforcer.py:475,497` and `merge_readiness.py`'s own `watch_progress_comment` (merge_readiness.py:894-916, a completely separate PR-sticky-comment watcher). Changing these keys' meaning for an event-driven coverage_enforcer redesign affects `merge_readiness.py` too unless you split the config.
- **Wrong-app drift detection requires a full snapshot, not a single event**: `drift_findings_for_terminal_runs` must see *every* check-run reporting a given context name (to catch a second/wrong GitHub App reporting the same context) — a design reacting to individual `check_run.completed` events one at a time still needs to re-fetch/hold the full check-runs list for the SHA at decision time; it cannot act on the triggering event's payload in isolation.
- **Expected-context set is not fixed at trigger time** — `active_expected_registry_checks` (line ~354-378) recomputes which contexts are currently required *every iteration*, because carry-forward/tag-run applicability depends on what's already visible in the check-runs list. A rewrite cannot compute "what am I waiting for" once at start; it must be re-evaluated at each decision point (whether that's a poll tick or an incoming event).
- **Trusted-checkout self-defense**: the calling workflow checks out `github.event.pull_request.base.sha || github.event.merge_group.base_sha` (`coverage-enforcer.yml:47`), i.e. always the **base** branch's copy of `coverage_enforcer.py`, never the PR head's copy — plus a grep-based bootstrap fail-closed guard (`coverage-enforcer.yml:63-68`) verifying the checked-out script still defines `expected_registry_checks_for_policy` before running. A rewrite must preserve running from a trusted base-branch checkout of itself; otherwise a PR could modify the very logic that gates it.
- **Step-summary/stdout is the only UI** — no check-run is published, so `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` (`write_step_summary`, 636-645) and stdout (`main`, 649-669) are the sole visible surface; a write failure to the step summary must warn but never flip a green verdict to failure (`assert_cli_summary_write_failure_warns_without_failing_green_verdict:749-798`).
- **Static registry/YAML derivation check is polling-independent** and already decoupled (`registry_workflow_derivation_findings`, called once per invocation, not per poll tick) — safe to carry over unchanged into any redesign; don't conflate it with the polling logic when refactoring.

External parsers only for: TOML configs (`tomllib`), `.mergify.yml` (a Ruby/Psych subprocess, MERGIFY_YAML_PARSER_RUBY @6393), git (subprocess in self-authorizing path).

Shared scanning helpers (the intended routes):
- `strip_comment` (1078) — quote-aware `#` stripping; primitive under everything.
- `uncommented_text` (2729) — standard "give me a job's searchable text."
- `parse_jobs` (1140) — `jobs:` → {id:[lines]} by exact 2-space indent.
- `top_level_block` (1173), `top_level_mapping_items` (3088), `scalar_mapping` (1197), `block_top_level_items` (3016), `block_nested_mapping_items` (3050).
- `step_blocks` (2231) → `action_blocks` (2279), `named_step_block` (3467), `setup_action_blocks` (2270).
- run-body: `block_run_commands` (1207), `block_run_body` (2973), `block_run_body_matches` (2997, PIN comparator via `normalize_script_text` 2960), `folded_yaml_run_commands` (9020), `workflow_run_shell_texts` (9400), `yaml_run_shell_texts` (9094).
- Shell tokenizer stack: `_command_tokens_cached` (3841, shlex.shlex w/ punctuation_chars) → `command_tokens` (3850) → `command_tokens_with_line_boundaries` (3854); `shell_logical_lines` (3990); command-substitution/backtick payload extractors (3869/3909/3941).

**Do families bypass the shared scanners? Yes — the core debt.** There are effectively **5 independent YAML-ish parsers**: (a) the main line-scanner, (b) a SEPARATE self-authorizing permissions sub-parser (`yaml_permissions_block_scopes` 10495, `yaml_flow_mapping_grants` 10520), (c) `_normalize_concurrency_text` (1258), (d) `no_mistakes_commands` (6203, its own anchor/alias-aware mini-parser), (e) the mergify Ruby subprocess — plus 1 shell tokenizer and tomllib. Many families also re-derive text via ad-hoc `uncommented_text(job_lines)` + substring `in` rather than structured lookups. **A single structured parse feeding the engine is the highest-leverage structural change.**

## 5. Test-side map (`test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py`, 17,779 lines, 217 defs)
Overwhelmingly **differential**. `assert_error(fragment, workflow=…)` (1761) runs verify_text, asserts one error fragment; `assert_clean` (1739) asserts base passes. Mutation primitives: `replace_once` (2741, fails loud if absent), `replace_once_after` (2774), `without_job` (2730), `without_once_after` (2783), `replace_config_key_line_once` (2747).

Census (`git grep -c`): negative assertions = **322 assert_error + 6 assert_workflows_error + 13 assert_nextest_error + 17 assert_artifact_retention_error + 11 assert_test_harness_manifest_error = 369**. Base mutations = **588 replace_once + 57 replace_once_after + 9 others ≈ 654**. assert_clean anchors = 10.

The dominant test is literally `assert_error("<msg>", replace_once(BASE_WORKFLOW, "<pinned literal>", "<corrupted>"))` — **the exact inverse of a PIN-∈ rule**. For the ~430 PIN-∈ + ~120 EQ + ~50 FORBID rules, each test is **auto-generable from the rule table** (synthesize violation → assert paired message). Estimate: **~75–80% of the 369 negative assertions (~280) auto-generable.**

Bespoke engine tests that CANNOT be generated (the EXPR tail, ~90 assertions / ~30–40 functions): self-authorizing governance (10 `init_self_authorizing_fixture_repo`, 16 `run_repo_git`, 16 `commit_repo`; `assert_self_authorizing_governance_detector_contract` 1859 spans ~650 lines); CI-policy matrix/resolver agreement (`assert_ci_policy_matrix` 3070, `assert_ci_policy_resolvers_agree` 3409); sccache subprocess (`_run_test_archive_build_script` 4486, retry test 4543); mergify Ruby round-trips; config-loader error paths (31 tempfile, 48 tmp_path, 7 subprocess.run, 7 importlib). **Split ≈ 280 auto-generable : 90 bespoke.**

## 6. Error-message inventory + external consumers
**Format:** overwhelmingly **ad-hoc hand-written literals**, one unique string per check. 243 of 616 append sites use f-strings parameterized by a loop var (`f"missing required job {job}"`, `f"{job} needs {dep}"`, `f"gate shared verdict call must include {required_arg}"`, `f"repo automation must not compile {tool} from source"`); the rest are fixed literals. **No shared message-template registry** — which forces the test side to hard-code 369 fragment literals.

**External consumers of exact error text: NONE.** `main` (15895–15900) prints `f"ERROR: {error}"` to stderr, returns exit 1. Invokers — ci.yml:410 (test target), ci.yml:454 (self-authorizing-governance subcommand), justfile:581/:503, merge_queue_preflight.py, backtester-ci.yml (comments only) — all treat it as **pass/fail by exit code**. `git grep` for distinctive message fragments outside the two files returns only the workflows' own `full_ci_required` expressions (which the verifier checks *for*, not consumers of its output). Error strings are a **private contract with the test file's substring matches only** — freely restructurable (e.g., into a uniform `{rule_id}: {detail}` template) as long as the ~369 test fragments regenerate from the same rule table; no downstream tooling breaks.

## Bottom line for the redesign
- **~430 of ~750 rules are PIN-∈** — one engine + one table replaces ~35 families and auto-generates ~280 tests.
- EQ (~120), FORBID (~50), CLASSIFY (~40) also table-izable with 3 more primitives.
- ~16 CROSS families need a "load file B, compare to A" primitive keyed on shared constants (many source from runners.toml).
- 9 EXPR functions stay as code; 2 could become new RESOLVE / SHELL-DATAFLOW primitives; the git-diff governance detector stays hand-written.
- **Hidden debt = the parser**: 5 independent YAML-ish parsers + 1 shell tokenizer, families re-scanning raw text via substring `in`. Unify the parse first.
- **One drift finding to fix in passing**: GATE_FULL/ITERATION/NOOP/DEFER_CONDITION + GATE_*_CONTEXT_FAILURE_CONDITION (10009–10017) are dead — defined, never referenced (verified `git grep` at SHA); `gate_policy_truth_table_errors` is flat EQ, not a policy_path truth table.
</agent-message>

# CI-DX: Python governance speed, debuggability, and kernel consolidation — audit + design

Child of #1068. Owner: Claude (design/review); Codex executes. All anchors at main `54044f0e9df1fedf228cb15c6ca04d5430c92adc` unless stated. Baseline measured 2026-07-04 (macOS dev machine, python3.12).

## Measured baseline

- `just ci-lint-workflow` battery = 27 sequential suites, **~6.2 min** wall. Pareto: `test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` 195s (53%), `test_merge_queue_preflight.py` 82s (22%), `test_rust_verification_cache_retention.py` 61s (16%) — top 3 = 91%.
- Production verifier (`verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py`) end-to-end: **2.9s**. One in-test `verify_text` pass: **~0.18s**; the hygiene test runs ~369 negative assertions (~654 mutations), each a full verify — that multiplication IS the 195s.
- `source-fence-static-inner` = **93 separate python3 interpreter spawns**; ≥5 fences each do independent full `rglob` walks of the Rust tree.
- Multi-session slowness root: `lane_governor` heavy lane is single-flight per machine (correct design, kernel-released flock; CI bypasses it). Concurrent sessions serialize behind each other's ~6-min batteries — a third session can queue 12+ min before its own run. Fix = make the battery fast, not touch the lock.
- Sandbox stall: `test_ci_provenance.py` redirect test (`assert_github_api_bytes_strips_authorization_on_cross_host_redirect`, :3407-3456) binds two real TCP servers; worst case 60s (2×30s hops, no retry) if a sandbox black-holes the handshake; also 93 `importlib` reloads of the 3,275-line module per suite run.

## Debt register (audit of all 165 scripts/*.py, 151,793 lines; 6-agent sweep, findings verified with file:line)

**Class A — "shared helper exists, copies drift, one copy loses a guard" (the #1 class; 2 live defects already attributable):**
1. GitHub HTTP clients ×3 + canonical: `cancel_obsolete_dispatch_runs.py:109` uses bare urlopen WITHOUT `SafeGitHubRedirectHandler` → Authorization header not stripped on cross-host redirect (token-leak gap). Canonical client: `ci_provenance.py:1471-1531`.
2. `nextest_fingerprint.py:142-146` local `require_positive_int` dropped the shared validator's bool guard → `shards = true` yields a nonsense fingerprint instead of failing closed (bool subclasses int). Untested gap at `test_nextest_fingerprint.py:648-663`.
3. `strip_rust_comments_and_literals` re-implemented 9× across verify_ra_*/verify_bte_* fences with ≥3 diverging bug surfaces; shared `rust_source_scanner.py` imported by exactly 1 file; a 5th superset variant (`production_text`) lives in `verify_bolt_v3_pure_rust_runtime.py` and is imported as a library by 8 sibling fences.
4. 3 independent sha256-digest impls; the hot path (`ci_input_sets.digest_input_set` :161-180, used by 3 workflows) reads raw bytes while `nextest_fingerprint.tree_digest` uses cheaper git object IDs.
5. 3 independent validators of `ci/rust-verification.toml` schema (rust_verification.py, verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py, scripts/cargo-shim).
6. Byte-identical duplicate fns rust_verification.py:3201-3229 vs ci_provenance.py:249-283; 11 helper functions intentionally divergent between rust_verification.py and the hygiene verifier, pinned as divergent by `test_command_understanding.py:457-558`.
7. Config validators hand-rolled in clean_merged_artifacts.py:255-308 (and forked `as_text` semantics in cancel_obsolete_dispatch_runs.py:127); no shared test-fixture module anywhere in scripts/ (load_owner_module etc. ×3).
8. 5 independent YAML-ish parsers inside the hygiene verifier itself.

**Class B — misplaced / dead:**
- 2,425 lines (57%) of `test_lane_governor.py` are two production-grade repo-invariant engines (`_RepoSharedStateWriteAnalyzer` :304-1584, `_CodeExecutionEdgeResolver` :1585-2728) powering a handful of tests — belongs in dedicated verify_*.py fences.
- Dead: GATE_FULL/ITERATION/NOOP/DEFER_CONDITION + context-failure consts (verifier :10009-10017, referenced nowhere); duplicate `run_display_title` def (rust_verification.py:3490 vs :3951 — first is shadowed); `merge_readiness.required_context_aliases` :251-272; `clean_merged_artifacts.SHORT_SHA_RE` :64; `ci_input_sets` `list` subcommand (no callers).
- `verify_ai_review_governance.py` golden-masters ~250 byte-exact YAML snippets (:16-323) + inline self-tests — brittle coupling + a second testing convention inside one family.
- Split ownership of "who may set BOLT_LOCAL_VERIFICATION_GATE=1" across local_verification_gate.py:44 / verifier :6721-6795 / test_lane_governor.py:1337 — no single owner.
- Unbounded `fcntl.flock` wait, no timeout/diagnostic: `rust_verification.py cache_lock` :814-822 (hang risk distinct from the well-behaved lane lock).

**Healthy (no action):** storage family layering (tripwire imports auditor — SSOT working), lane_governor design, fences' fail-loud discipline (zero fail-open findings in all six families beyond the two Class-A defects), research scripts confirmed non-CI.

## Verifier taxonomy (the design foundation)

~750–900 rules in the 15,916-line verifier. Kinds: **PIN-∈** (pinned literal present/absent in a scoped region) ~430 rules/35 families — the dominant shape; EQ ~120; CROSS ~90 (16 families, mostly keyed on runners.toml); FORBID ~50; CLASSIFY ~40; whole-body PIN ~10; **EXPR (irreducible custom) ~15 rules / 9 functions** (git-diff self-authorization correlator, shell dataflow reachability, raw-cargo wrapper tokenizer, if-chain parser, git-archive arg analysis, retention DSL, shard arithmetic, concurrency normalizer, aarch64 guard glue). Test side: 369 negative assertions, ~280 (75-80%) mechanically derivable from a rule table; ~90 bespoke stay. Error text has **zero external consumers** (exit-code contract only; grep-verified) — messages may be restructured to `{rule_id}: {detail}`.

## Design

**WS1 — Shared kernel + adoption fence.** Create/consolidate: `github_client` (promote ci_provenance's client + SafeGitHubRedirectHandler; adopt in cancel_obsolete_dispatch_runs, merge_readiness; clean_merged stays gh-CLI by design or migrates later), `config_validators` (exists — enforce adoption; fix nextest_fingerprint bool bug + add bool-value test), `rust_source_scanner` (absorb `production_text` as reference impl; retire the 9 fence copies), `digests` (git-oid based; ci_input_sets adopts), single `rust-verification.toml` schema owner (rust_verification.load_policy; other two import), shared `scripts/test_fixtures.py`. **Class closure:** a fence rule forbidding definition of kernel symbol names outside kernel modules (extends the existing fence pattern), so copies can't silently return.

**WS2 — Rule engine for the hygiene verifier (consolidation, NOT decomposition).**
- `workflow_model.py`: ONE structured parse per file. The proven scanners (`parse_jobs`, `step_blocks`, `block_run_body*`, `strip_comment`, shell tokenizer stack) are MOVED, not rewritten — parser semantics are security-load-bearing.
- `contract_rules.py`: the table — frozen rows `(id, kind, file_scope, selector, payload_const, message)`. Pinned constants remain reviewed Python literals (they ARE the tamper contract).
- `contract_engine.py`: evaluators for PIN, PIN-∈, EQ, CLASSIFY, FORBID, CROSS (+ optional RESOLVE for the retention DSL). Fail-closed: parse failure or missing selector target = error, never skip.
- `verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py` stays the entry point (CLI + `self-authorizing-governance` subcommand byte-compatible); EXPR residue (~9 functions) stays hand-written inside it with existing bespoke tests.
- Generated differential tests: for every table rule, synthesize the violating mutation and assert exactly that rule id fires; assert_clean on real files; meta-test asserts every rule is falsifiable (no vacuous rule — same inverted-contract pattern as #1172/#1208). ~280 hand-written assertions retire; ~90 bespoke remain.
- **Migration manifest**: every one of the ~90 family functions and 616 error-emission sites mapped to rule ids or explicitly retained-EXPR; a completeness check asserts full accounting so no rule is lost in translation. Strangler tranches (~6 PRs by cluster), each: migrate families → delete old code → regenerate tests → adversarial self-review; external model panel on the final tranche. Every tranche PR refuses archive reuse on its own runs (expected — verifier is in the detector pathspec).
- Expected outcome: verifier ~16k → ~5-6k lines; test ~17.8k → ~4-5k; hygiene suite 195s → seconds-to-tens (rule-scoped evaluation replaces full re-verify per assert); net LOC sharply DOWN (explicit anti-goal: no scattering).

**WS3 — Battery & runner mechanics.**
- `run_fences.py`: one process imports all fence modules via registry, one FS walk + shared text cache, per-fence loud reporting; per-file CLIs retained for solo debugging. 93 spawns → 1.
- Parallel battery: ci-lint-workflow-inner runs suites concurrently (bounded by cores), loud aggregate; later, internal sharding of remaining big suites.
- Micro-fixes: TCP redirect test fails IMMEDIATELY with "needs network permission" under sandbox denial (never silent-skip, never 60s); cache the ci_provenance module load (93 reloads → 1); bound `cache_lock` flock wait with timeout + holder diagnostic.
- lane_governor unchanged; fast battery dissolves the queueing.

**WS4 — Debuggability (from the CI-DX pillar; folded into tranches).** Failure surfacing first (wrapper scripts emit failing step + exit code + relevant lines as ::error — exemplar: nextest partition wrapper); $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY decision lines (run classification, reuse decision + cause, S3 eligible/assumed/hit-miss+reason) land WITH the engine tranches that own those pinned step bodies, to avoid double-touching verifier pins.

**WS5 — coverage-enforcer redesign (last; $ already reduced by #1203).** Hybrid adaptive polling honoring the 7 documented constraints (fail-closed 4h deadline, never publish check-runs, base-tree self-checkout, full-snapshot drift detection, per-iteration expected-set recompute, shared TOML keys with merge_readiness must be split first, step-summary-only UI). Full event-driven rejected: no reliable event→PR correlation for merge-queue refs.

## Phasing

- **P0 (1 short PR series, immediate):** the safety/latency micro-fixes — token-leak client adoption in cancel_obsolete_dispatch_runs; nextest_fingerprint bool bug + test; TCP fast-fail; ci_provenance test module-load cache; cache_lock timeout. Independent, tiny, each closes a live defect.
- **P1 (tactical speed):** parallel battery + run_fences.py + shared test fixtures. Target: ci-lint battery ≤ ~3.3 min (bounded by hygiene suite), fence battery interpreter overhead eliminated. Before/after at same commit in PR bodies.
- **P2 (strategic):** WS2 engine tranches with migration manifest. Target: battery ≤ ~1.5 min after hygiene collapse; verifier+test LOC roughly halved or better.
- **P3 (parallel-safe with P2):** kernel adoption sweep (WS1 remainder: 9× stripper retirement, digest/schema unification, extract the two engines from test_lane_governor.py into verify_*.py fences, gate-env single owner, dead-code deletions).
- **P4:** WS5 coverage-enforcer + preflight polish (single policy validation per just invocation).

## Not in scope
#1070/F2 fallback adjudication (runs as its own lane; note: this audit found ZERO fail-open debt in the six CI families — F2's remaining surface is Rust-side and non-CI scripts). Rust monolith decomposition. verify_ai_review_governance golden-master refactor (flagged; own item after WS2 proves the pattern).

## Acceptance (epic level)
1. Battery wall-clock: 6.2 min → ≤1.5 min measured at same commit; multi-session lane queueing correspondingly shrunk.
2. Verifier + hygiene test combined LOC reduced ≥50% with the migration manifest proving zero rules lost; every table rule proven falsifiable by generated differential.
3. Kernel fence live: re-defining kernel symbols outside kernel fails CI.
4. The two live defects (token redirect, bool fingerprint) fixed with regression tests.
5. A failed CI job names its failing step + reason in the job summary/annotation (no more exit-1 archaeology).

---

# The audit is complete and the design is filed — epic **#1215**

**First, today's merges:** #1211 is in (merged batched with incident-campaign Rust work, so its cache-restore check was the documented "batched" miss — correct behavior, new fingerprint now being stored; first *hit* expected on the upcoming justfile-only PR, which by design can't disturb the fingerprint). **#1210 is now 100% delivered** — all five bullets shipped or applied. Say the word and I'll close it with the evidence comment.

## What the full audit found (all 165 Python files, ~152k lines)

- **The #1 debt class, confirmed everywhere: copies drift.** Shared helpers exist but get re-implemented — 9 copies of one function in the fences, 3 GitHub clients, 3 config validators, 3 schema validators, 5 mini-parsers inside the giant. This produced **two live defects**: a token-leak gap (one client copy skipped the auth-stripping protection) and the fingerprint bug (`true` accepted as a number). Your instinct about "bad things spread out" was right — just at the helper level, not the fallback level: **zero fail-open/fallback debt was found**; the fail-loud discipline is genuinely good.
- **The slowness is 3 files, not 165**: three test suites are 91% of the 6-minute battery, and the giant's suite is slow because it re-runs the full verifier ~370 times.
- **The 25-minute session stalls are queuing, not computing**: concurrent sessions serialize behind each other's 6-minute batteries on a (correctly designed) one-at-a-time lock. Fast battery ⇒ queue dissolves.
- **The giant is 98% table-izable**: ~750–900 rules, of which only ~15 are genuinely custom logic. ~280 of its 369 hand-written tests can be *generated* from the rule table. Error messages have zero external consumers, so restructuring is free.

## The design (full version in #1215)

One shared kernel + one rule engine + generated tests + parallel batteries — consolidation, with line count going **down**, plus a fence that forbids re-creating kernel copies so the class stays closed. Targets: battery 6.2 min → ≤1.5 min, verifier+test lines cut ≥50% with a migration manifest proving zero rules lost, failures that name themselves.

## First execution handoff (P0 — the five safety/latency micro-fixes, one PR)

```

no close-keywords, "Addresses #1215", create PR never merge, python3.12, never cancel/rerun CI).

FIX 1 — Token-redirect hardening (#1215 Class A item 1).
scripts/cancel_obsolete_dispatch_runs.py builds its own urllib client and calls urlopen directly
(~:109) WITHOUT the SafeGitHubRedirectHandler that ci_provenance.py's canonical client uses —
Authorization is not stripped on a cross-host redirect. Fix: route its requests through the
canonical opener/handler from ci_provenance (import, don't copy). Regression test: in-process
assertion that the opener chain includes the redirect-safety handler / that headers are stripped
on a simulated cross-host redirect — do NOT add another real-TCP test.

FIX 2 — Fingerprint bool bug (#1215 Class A item 2).
scripts/nextest_fingerprint.py:142-146 local require_positive_int lacks the isinstance(value, bool)
guard the shared scripts/config_validators.require_positive_int has, so `shards = true` produces a
nonsense fingerprint instead of failing closed. Fix: delete the local copy, import the shared one.
Test: boolean shards value → loud failure (extend the family at test_nextest_fingerprint.py:648-663).

FIX 3 — Sandbox TCP fast-fail.
scripts/test_ci_provenance.py:3407-3456 (assert_github_api_bytes_strips_authorization_on_cross_host
_redirect) binds two real TCP servers; under a black-hole sandbox each HTTP hop can stall 30s (2
hops = 60s). Fix: explicit short socket/request timeouts (~5s) scoped to THIS test plus a clear
failure message ("requires local TCP permission"). It must FAIL loud when it cannot run — never
silently skip (repo fail-loud policy); the win is failing in seconds with a self-explanatory
message instead of a silent minute.

FIX 4 — Module-load caching in test_ci_provenance.py.
The suite importlib-reloads the 3,275-line ci_provenance module 93 times per run. Fix: load once
and reuse. CAUTION: first verify no test mutates module globals relying on a fresh copy — if any
does, give those tests an explicit fresh-load helper and cache the rest. Prove no cross-test
contamination by a clean full-suite run before/after, and report the suite's wall-clock delta.

FIX 5 — Bound the cache lock wait.
scripts/rust_verification.py cache_lock (:814-822) does a blocking fcntl.flock with NO timeout —
a wedged holder blocks `just test`/`just clippy` forever with no diagnostic. Fix: non-blocking
probe + poll loop with deadline and a periodic "waiting for cache lock held by <pid/cmdline if
discoverable>" heartbeat, timing out with a loud error (mirror lane_governor's acquire() shape and
reuse its policy durations rather than inventing new constants). Update the lock-holder tests in
test_rust_verification_cache_retention.py (the sleep-1 shim tests at ~:1373/:1452) accordingly.

VERIFY: python3.12 on every touched suite (test_ci_provenance, test_nextest_fingerprint,
test_rust_verification_cache_retention, test_cancel_obsolete_dispatch_runs) + just ci-lint-workflow
+ adversarial self-review (fixes 1-2 are security-adjacent). Report per-fix: what changed, test
evidence, and for fix 4 the measured before/after suite time. PR body links issue #1215.

Reconciled and recorded. The plain-English summary of where this leaves us:

## The headline

**The campaign's dollar effect is now measured, not estimated: ~$58.6/day → ~$11.2/day (−81%)** on the three material workflows, computed from actual job durations × published machine rates. That's roughly **$1,400/month** of burn eliminated. (Properly caveated as a lower-bound comparison — some old runs had unmappable machine labels.)

## What Codex's measurements confirmed or corrected

- **Confirmed my diagnosis** of the slow test suite: one helper (`assert_error`) accounts for 81 of the 195 seconds across 371 calls — the exact multiplication the rule-engine design eliminates.
- **Corrected one of my claims**: I said "clippy is the wall-clock floor"; the data shows build *and* clippy are twin ~11.5-minute floors, and the run I'd cited was actually tailed by a cache miss. Accepted and amended in the epic.
- **Settled the "buy more machines?" question for now**: the horrifying queue waits (up to ~90 min) all cluster in the July 1–2 storm era — which we already fixed. Verdict: don't spend; remeasure after the metrics week.

## The board now

- **#1215** — design authority (my audit + architecture). **#1213** — measurement record + PR tracker. Reconciled, no overlap, both cross-linked.
- **Approved execution order**: the four small **debuggability PRs first** (your priority — failures that explain themselves), the P0 five-fix PR (already dispatched) and the battery parallelization in parallel, then the engine tranches, then coverage-enforcer last.

Nothing needed from you right now. The next deliverables arriving for my review: the P0 PR and the first debuggability PR.
but that's still expensive because it's still $350

You're right to push — $11/day ≈ $340/month is still real money. Here's where it goes and what's still coming out of it:

**Decomposition of the $11.21/day:** ~$8.2 is the main CI's heavy ARM machines, ~$1.5 backtester, ~$1.5 coverage-enforcer残. The heavy-machine number means ~65 full proofs a day at ~45 heavy-minutes each. Two facts follow:

1. **Cost now scales with development activity, not waste.** The $58/day era was machines spinning on *nothing* (duplicate storms, cache thrash, idle polling). Today's $11 is mostly real compilation triggered by real work — two AI campaigns pushing and dispatching all day. On a quiet day this drops toward ~$1–2 by itself.

2. **Three reducers are already in flight** that cut the *per-proof* price:
 - **Cache restore-hits** (the thing we're one clean merge away from): turns the ~11-minute test-build into a ~1-minute download whenever Rust didn't change → biggest single per-proof cut.
 - **The fence-battery consolidation** (P1): the `source-fence` job burns ~9 heavy-minutes per proof running 93 separate Python processes; one process + one filesystem walk should roughly halve it or better.
 - **Coverage-enforcer redesign** (P4): the remaining ~$1.5/day of polling → ~$0.15.

 Realistic landing zone at *current* activity: **~$5–6/day**, i.e. ~$150–180/month.

3. **The last lever is usage policy, not engineering**: a chunk of those 65 daily proofs are the incident campaign dispatching *full* CI on every iteration for evidence. If intermediate iterations used the cheap lane and only the final head got the full dispatch, proof count drops materially. That's a working-practice call for the other campaign — I can write the one-paragraph recommendation for it if you want it enforced, but I'd rather not fence another session's workflow without you deciding that.

So: $350/month isn't the destination — it's the mid-campaign reading. The honest floor is ~half that at this intensity, and far less when the campaigns wind down.

**Layer 1 — Your Mac: thinking only.** Agents' reasoning, file edits, and checks that run in *seconds*. Nothing that compiles, nothing that runs minutes. **Layer 2 — Ubicloud: the elastic work floor.** Every heavy task — compile, test, lint, debug iteration — is a dispatched remote job, one runner per task, agents never sharing or queuing on each other for *iteration* work. 10 agents debugging simultaneously = 10 runners at ~$0.002/min ≈ pennies. The harness itself is well built: single-process discovery, per-fence loud failure with traceback, argv isolation, lane acquired once, FS-cache hit-stats, self-tests for each property, and the per-fence wiring self-checks correctly retargeted to the new recipe shape. The blocking problem is scope loss, not design.

**F1 — BLOCKING: the battery dropped ~50 test suites.** The old `source-fence-static-inner` ran each fence's `test_verify_*.py` self-test PLUS standalone suites (`test_lane_governor.py`, `test_local_verification_gate.py`, `test_verify_runtime_capture_yaml.py`, the two `test_migrate_*` suites). The new recipe is only `python3 scripts/run_fences.py`, which discovers `verify_*.py` only — and the new verifier pin ("must contain only run_fences.py") now FORBIDS re-adding them. Consequences: (a) every fence's differential self-test (the proof it can fail) no longer runs anywhere in CI — the vacuous-fence class returns; (b) `test_lane_governor.py` embeds two repo-wide invariant engines (`_RepoSharedStateWriteAnalyzer`, `_CodeExecutionEdgeResolver` — see #1215 audit) whose enforcement just silently stopped; (c) the 194s→32.4s number conflates real speedup with deleted work.
Fix: run_fences must ALSO run the paired `test_verify_*.py` suites plus the dropped standalone suites in-process (they are all `main()`-shaped and import-runnable, same as the fences), OR they must be explicitly re-homed with the verifier pin updated to match — nothing may simply vanish. Then re-measure and report the honest before/after with coverage equal on both sides.

**F2 — MUST FIX in same PR: FS-cache staleness hazard.** `shared_filesystem_cache` monkeypatches `pathlib.Path.read_text/glob/rglob` process-wide keyed by resolved path. Safe for read-only fences; WRONG for anything that writes-then-rereads (exactly what test fixtures do, e.g. write policy → module rereads it). With F1's fix bringing tests in-process, the cache MUST NOT be active during test-suite execution — and as a class guard, restrict caching to paths under REPO_ROOT (tempdir fixtures then bypass it structurally, not by convention).

**N2 (note):** `run_fence` prints OK/FAIL to stderr; fine, but keep stdout clean-contract documented in the module docstring so future summary tooling knows which stream to parse.

Evidence bar for round 2: same-commit before/after wall-clock for `just source-fence-static` AND confirmation that every suite present in the old 93-line recipe is executed somewhere (list the mapping old-line → new-home in the PR body). Checks green is necessary but not sufficient here — the whole point of F1 is that green stays green when coverage silently drops.

1. COVERAGE COMPLETENESS — round-1 sin is fixed. Refuted.

Old (93 invocations)    New home
44 verify_*.py    discover_fence_paths (run_fences.py:166) — identical 44-element set

Net: 44 fences (unchanged set) + 50 tests (49 old + 1 new self-test). Nothing dropped; nothing inappropriate added. Exclusion prefixes (run_fences.py:29 verify_ai_/verify_ci_/verify_runtime_capture_yaml) match exactly the lanes that own them. The round-1 "unscoped cache" is also fixed: cache is repo-root-scoped (run_fences.py:62 cacheable_path) and outside-root reads bypass it (proven by test_run_fences.py::assert_filesystem_cache_skips_paths_outside_root).
2. CACHE SAFETY — sound for the actual battery.
- Monkeypatch restore is in finally (run_fences.py:151-152) — no permanent pathlib mutation, even on exception.
- glob/rglob return iter(tuple) — fresh iterator each call, kwargs passed through (run_fences.py:70-74,113-118). Iterator/kwargs semantics preserved.
- Stale-serve / write-then-reread: I grepped every discovered fence for file mutation (write_text/open('w')/json.dump/shutil/mkdir/subprocess). The only hits were dataclasses.replace (in-memory), json.dumps (in-memory), and read-only git show/git rev-parse (verify_bolt_v3_boundary_evidence.py:469, verify_bolt_v3_dependency_direction.py:890). ## DESIGN: fast remote debug lane (WS6) — priority raised to top by owner 2026-07-05

**Problem:** debugging iteration costs a full CI round trip (12-17 min, serialized behind other proofs) per hypothesis. Measured exhibit: Lane-4 session, 1h38m for one failure. This is now the #1 development-speed constraint.

**Goal:** any agent tests one hypothesis on its own rented runner in ~3-6 min, N agents fully parallel, zero load on the dev machine, cost ~1 cent/run.

**Shape — one new workflow, `debug-test.yml`:**
- Trigger: `workflow_dispatch` only. Inputs: `ref` (branch), `filter` (nextest filter expression), optional `package`. One-liner for agents: `gh workflow run debug-test.yml -f ref=<branch> -f filter='test(my_test_name)'`.
- Runner: `${{ vars.CI_RUNNER_MANAGED_HEAVY }}` (same ARM tier — fingerprint/arch parity). `timeout-minutes: 30`. No concurrency group (parallel dispatches by design; each run independent).
- Steps: checkout ref → setup-environment → sccache via the PR-readonly role (dispatch AssumeRole works since the 07-04 IAM trust widening; warm sccache = only changed crates compile) → optional S3 archive restore if the digest matches (free when it does) → run the FILTERED test set through a new managed justfile recipe (`debug-test FILTER [PACKAGE]` → `cargo nextest run -E FILTER --locked` under managed env, JOBS cap per policy) → job summary: pass/fail + failing-test names + last relevant log lines (debuggability format, not a 3000-line dump).

**Hard security/governance constraints (non-negotiable, verifier-enforced):**
1. `permissions: contents: read` ONLY. No provenance emission, no check-runs, no gate interaction, never required-capable, never referenced by .mergify.yml or ruleset — structurally incapable of authorizing a merge.
2. Cache access read-only (PR-readonly role only; no write role reference anywhere in the workflow).
3. The cargo invocation goes through a pinned managed justfile recipe consistent with the raw-cargo governance (repo_automation_raw_cargo_errors) — no raw cargo in the workflow body.
4. Hygiene-verifier contract for the new workflow: pinned envelope (triggers, permissions, runner var, timeout, the managed-recipe call line), same PIN pattern as sibling workflows, with differential tests. The workflow must also be excluded from reuse-candidate sources (it emits no provenance, so ci_provenance's require_gate_check already excludes it — verify with a fixture, don't assume).
5. Runner-minutes exposure bounded: timeout 30 min + dispatch-only trigger. No cron.

**Usage contract (the $-and-speed rule, stated in the workflow header comment):** iteration happens here; full CI runs only at merge time and for final pre-merge evidence. This is what takes steady-state cost from ~$5-6/day to ~$1.5-2/day at full intensity — the engineering makes it possible, the contract makes it real. Operator relays the contract line to all agent-campaign briefs.

**Explicitly rejected alternatives:** local cargo iteration (rejected by owner: local CPU contention was a historical development-speed disaster; lane-lock serialization just relocates the queue); a shared always-on debug runner (state pollution, idle cost); reusing ci.yml with an input flag (couples the gate machinery to a non-gating path — the #1162/#1165 lesson is to keep decision surfaces small).

**Acceptance:** (1) dispatch on a branch with a deliberately failing test → run completes ≤6 min warm, summary names the failing test + tail; (2) two dispatches from different branches run CONCURRENTLY (no mutual queueing) — run IDs + timestamps as evidence; (3) hygiene verifier green with the new contract + differential tests; (4) a run on a ref with matching digest restores the archive instead of compiling (when available — do not block acceptance on batch luck); (5) merge-gating behavior of everything else unchanged (full drain green).

152	+#!/usr/bin/env python3
153	+"""Run ci-lint workflow suites with bounded parallel subprocess workers."""
154	+
155	+from __future__ import annotations
156	+
157	+import argparse
158	+import dataclasses
159	+import pathlib
160	+import subprocess
161	+import sys
162	+from collections.abc import Iterable
163	+from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
164	+from typing import TextIO
165	+
166	+
167	+REPO_ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
168	+DEFAULT_WORKERS = 4
169	+MAX_WORKERS = 6
170	+
171	+
172	+@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
173	+class CiLintSuite:
174	+    name: str
175	+    command: tuple[str, ...]
176	+
177	+
178	+@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
179	+class SuiteResult:
180	+    suite: CiLintSuite
181	+    returncode: int
182	+    stdout: str
183	+    stderr: str
184	+
185	+
186	+CI_LINT_SUITES = (
187	+    CiLintSuite("ci-workflow-hygiene-tests", ("python3", "scripts/test_verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py")),
188	+    CiLintSuite("ci-test-manifest", ("python3", "scripts/test_ci_test_manifest.py")),
189	+    CiLintSuite("cancel-obsolete-dispatch-runs", ("python3", "scripts/test_cancel_obsolete_dispatch_runs.py")),
190	+    CiLintSuite("config-validators", ("python3", "scripts/test_config_validators.py")),
191	+    CiLintSuite("run-rust-probe", ("python3", "scripts/test_run_rust_probe.py")),
192	+    CiLintSuite("rust-probe-wrapper", ("python3", "scripts/test_rust_probe_wrapper.py")),
193	+    CiLintSuite("ci-provenance", ("python3", "scripts/test_ci_provenance.py")),
194	+    CiLintSuite("ci-input-sets", ("python3", "scripts/test_ci_input_sets.py")),
195	+    CiLintSuite("rust-test-targets", ("python3", "scripts/test_rust_test_targets.py")),
196	+    CiLintSuite("merge-readiness", ("python3", "scripts/test_merge_readiness.py")),
197	+    CiLintSuite("merge-queue-preflight", ("python3", "scripts/test_merge_queue_preflight.py")),
198	+    CiLintSuite("merge-queue-operator", ("python3", "scripts/test_merge_queue_operator.py")),
199	+    CiLintSuite("coverage-enforcer", ("python3", "scripts/test_coverage_enforcer.py")),
200	+    CiLintSuite("nextest-fingerprint", ("python3", "scripts/test_nextest_fingerprint.py")),
201	+    CiLintSuite("root-bin-sidecars", ("python3", "scripts/test_root_bin_sidecars.py")),
202	+    CiLintSuite("ci-storage-audit", ("python3", "scripts/test_ci_storage_audit.py")),
203	+    CiLintSuite("ci-storage-tripwire", ("python3", "scripts/test_ci_storage_tripwire.py")),
204	+    CiLintSuite("same-sha-main-evidence", ("python3", "scripts/test_find_same_sha_main_evidence.py")),
205	+    CiLintSuite("ubicloud-runner-minutes", ("python3", "scripts/test_ubicloud_runner_minutes.py")),
206	+    CiLintSuite("verify-ci-path-filters-tests", ("python3", "scripts/test_verify_ci_path_filters.py")),
207	+    CiLintSuite("rust-verification", ("python3", "scripts/test_rust_verification.py")),
208	+    CiLintSuite("verify-remote", ("python3", "scripts/test_verify_remote.py")),
209	+    CiLintSuite("command-understanding", ("python3", "scripts/test_command_understanding.py")),
210	+    CiLintSuite("rust-verification-decoupling", ("python3", "scripts/test_rust_verification_decoupling.py")),
211	+    CiLintSuite("rust-verification-cache-retention", ("python3", "scripts/test_rust_verification_cache_retention.py")),
212	+    CiLintSuite("verify-ci-path-filters", ("python3", "scripts/verify_ci_path_filters.py")),
213	+    CiLintSuite("ci-workflow-hygiene-verifier", ("python3", "scripts/verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py")),
214	+    CiLintSuite("run-ci-lint-suites", ("python3", "scripts/test_run_ci_lint_suites.py")),
215	+)
216	+
217	+
218	+def validate_workers(workers: int) -> int:
219	+    if workers < 1 or workers > MAX_WORKERS:
220	+        raise ValueError(f"workers must be between 1 and {MAX_WORKERS}")
221	+    return workers
222	+
223	+
224	+def run_one_suite(suite: CiLintSuite, repo_root: pathlib.Path) -> SuiteResult:
225	+    try:
226	+        result = subprocess.run(
227	+            list(suite.command),
228	+            cwd=repo_root,
229	+            text=True,
230	+            stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
231	+            stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
232	+            check=False,
233	+        )
234	+    except OSError as exc:
235	+        return SuiteResult(suite=suite, returncode=127, stdout="", stderr=f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}\n")
236	+    return SuiteResult(suite=suite, returncode=result.returncode, stdout=result.stdout, stderr=result.stderr)
237	+
238	+
239	+def write_block(stream: TextIO, text: str) -> None:
240	+    if not text:
241	+        return
242	+    stream.write(text)
243	+    if not text.endswith("\n"):
244	+        stream.write("\n")
245	+
246	+
247	+def print_result(result: SuiteResult, *, stdout: TextIO, stderr: TextIO) -> None:
248	+    stdout.write(f"=== ci-lint suite: {result.suite.name} ===\n")
249	+    stdout.write(f"$ {' '.join(result.suite.command)}\n")
250	+    write_block(stdout, result.stdout)
251	+    write_block(stderr, result.stderr)
252	+    if result.returncode == 0:
253	+        stdout.write(f"OK: {result.suite.name}\n")
254	+    else:
255	+        stderr.write(f"FAIL: {result.suite.name} exited {result.returncode}\n")
256	+
257	+
258	+def run_suites(
259	+    suites: Iterable[CiLintSuite] = CI_LINT_SUITES,
260	+    *,
261	+    workers: int = DEFAULT_WORKERS,
262	+    repo_root: pathlib.Path = REPO_ROOT,
263	+    stdout: TextIO = sys.stdout,
264	+    stderr: TextIO = sys.stderr,
265	+) -> int:
266	+    worker_count = validate_workers(workers)
267	+    suite_list = tuple(suites)
268	+    if not suite_list:
269	+        return 0
270	+    results_by_index: dict[int, SuiteResult] = {}
271	+    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=worker_count) as executor:
272	+        futures = {executor.submit(run_one_suite, suite, repo_root): index for index, suite in enumerate(suite_list)}
273	+        for future in as_completed(futures):
274	+            result = future.result()
275	+            results_by_index[futures[future]] = result
276	+
277	+    failures: list[SuiteResult] = []
278	+    for index, suite in enumerate(suite_list):
279	+        result = results_by_index[index]
280	+        print_result(result, stdout=stdout, stderr=stderr)
281	+        if result.returncode != 0:
282	+            failures.append(result)
283	+
284	+    if failures:
285	+        stderr.write(f"FAIL: {len(failures)} ci-lint suite(s) failed:\n")
286	+        for result in failures:
287	+            stderr.write(f"- {result.suite.name} exited {result.returncode}\n")
288	+        return 1
289	+    stdout.write(f"OK: {len(suite_list)} ci-lint suite(s) passed.\n")
290	+    return 0
291	+
292	+
293	+def parse_args(argv: list[str]) -> argparse.Namespace:
294	+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
295	+    parser.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=DEFAULT_WORKERS)
296	+    parser.add_argument("--repo-root", type=pathlib.Path, default=REPO_ROOT)
297	+    parser.add_argument("--list", action="store_true", help="print suite commands without running them")
298	+    return parser.parse_args(argv)
299	+
300	+
301	+def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
302	+    args = parse_args(sys.argv[1:] if argv is None else argv)
303	+    if args.list:
304	+        for suite in CI_LINT_SUITES:
305	+            print(" ".join(suite.command))
306	+        return 0
307	+    return run_suites(workers=args.workers, repo_root=args.repo_root)
308	+
309	+
310	+if __name__ == "__main__":
311	+    raise SystemExit(main())

Findings (ranked)

F1 — LOW / non-blocking (diagnosability regression on the hang path). scripts/run_ci_lint_suites.py:120-135 (run_suites). All results are collected inside the with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) block (for future in as_completed(futures), :122) and printed only after it exits (:127-135). If one suite hangs, the as_completed loop and the executor's __exit__(wait=True) block on that future forever, so nothing is printed at all — not even the 27 completed suites — and there's no indication which suite is outstanding. Because output is captured (subprocess.PIPE), even a merely-slow suite streams nothing until it finishes. The old sequential recipe invoked python3 scripts/foo.py directly, streaming each suite live, so a hang was visible at the stuck suite. No per-suite timeout exists in either model (pre-existing), so a true infinite loop blocks until killed both ways — but the new model loses hang attribution. Failure scenario: a suite deadlocks after a future edit; the battery goes silent for the full run and the developer can't tell which of 28 suites is stuck. Given this PR is part of the CI-DX epic, worth fixing: emit a per-suite start/finish breadcrumb to stderr as futures are submitted/complete (keeps the grouped table-order final output intact, restores "which suite is outstanding"). Not a merge blocker — no correctness, coverage, or safety impact.

F2 — MINOR (narrow exception catch). scripts/run_ci_lint_suites.py:83 — run_one_suite catches only OSError. Any other exception from subprocess.run (e.g. UnicodeDecodeError if a suite emits non-UTF-8 to the text=True PIPE) propagates out of future.result() (:123) and aborts the entire battery with an unattributed traceback instead of failing just that suite. Low likelihood (Python self-tests on a UTF-8 locale), but it undercuts the "all failures reported, attributed" goal. Broadening to except Exception in run_one_suite (mapping to a nonzero SuiteResult) would close it.
